title: Biomolecules & Cell Biology — Detailed Study
notes:
Life Components

All living organisms are made up of complex chemical substances, which are continuously being synthesized and broken down.

Components of Life

  • Organic components: Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, nucleic acids, hormones.
  • Inorganic components: Water, minerals, gases.

Inorganic Components

Water

  • About 70–80% of the protoplasm of living cells is water.
  • Small and dipolar molecule — acts as a universal solvent.
  • Acts as a medium for biochemical reactions.

Minerals

Needed in small amounts for body functions. Common minerals: sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, iron, phosphorus, sulphur, iodine.

Biomolecules

Organic compounds synthesized by living organisms.

Carbohydrates

Polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones with the general formula Cn(H2O)n.

ClassExamplesFeatures
MonosaccharidesGlucose, fructose, galactose, riboseSimplest; cannot be hydrolyzed further.
OligosaccharidesSucrose, maltose, lactose2–10 monosaccharide units (disaccharides: 2 units).
PolysaccharidesStarch, glycogen, celluloseMany monosaccharide units; structural/energy storage roles.

Amino Acids

Organic compounds containing an amino group (−NH2) and a carboxyl group (−COOH).

General structure: R–CH(NH2)–COOH; linked by peptide bonds to form proteins. About 20 amino acids make up all proteins.

Proteins

Most abundant organic molecules of the cell.

  • Structure levels: Primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (α-helix, β-pleated sheet), tertiary (3D folding), quaternary (subunit assembly).
  • Functions: Structural support, catalysis (enzymes), transport, immunity (antibodies), muscle contraction (actin, myosin).

Lipids

Hydrophobic organic compounds (fats, oils, waxes, sterols).

  • Not polymers — built from glycerol and fatty acids via ester bonds.
  • Functions: Energy storage (9 kcal/g), cell membrane structure (phospholipids), insulation, hormone precursors.

Nucleic Acids

Nucleotides (pentose sugar + nitrogenous base + phosphate) linked by phosphodiester bonds.

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
BasesAdenine, Guanine, Cytosine, ThymineAdenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Uracil
StrandDouble-stranded (double helix)Single-stranded
LocationNucleus (chromosomes), mitochondria, plastidsNucleolus, cytoplasm, ribosomes
FunctionGenetic material; heredityProtein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA)

Enzymes

Biocatalysts — proteinaceous substances that speed up biochemical reactions without being consumed.

Characteristics:

  • Highly specific to their substrate.
  • Work best at an optimum temperature (about 37°C) and optimum pH.
  • Enzymes lower the activation energy of reactions.
  • They are reused — one enzyme molecule can act on many substrate molecules.

Naming: Usually end in -ase (e.g., sucrase, lipase, maltase).
examples:
**Q1: Polymer Linkages**

Which bonds link monomers in carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids respectively?

**Solution:** Glycosidic bonds in carbohydrates, peptide bonds in proteins, and phosphodiester bonds in nucleic acids.

**Q2: Protein Structure**

The α-helix and β-pleated sheet represent which level of protein organization?

**Solution:** Secondary structure. It arises from hydrogen bonding between the backbone atoms; the primary structure is the linear amino acid sequence held by peptide bonds.

**Q3: DNA vs RNA**

A nucleic acid contains ribose sugar and uracil. Is it DNA or RNA?

**Solution:** RNA. DNA contains deoxyribose and thymine instead; uracil pairs with adenine in RNA.

**Q4: Enzyme Properties**

Why can one enzyme molecule catalyze many substrate molecules?

**Solution:** Because enzymes are not consumed in reactions — they lower activation energy, bind substrate at the active site, and are released unchanged to act again.

keyPoints: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides → oligosaccharides → polysaccharides, joined by glycosidic bonds.
Proteins: 20 amino acids linked by peptide bonds; structure levels primary → secondary → tertiary → quaternary.
DNA: deoxyribose + A,G,C,T, double-stranded; RNA: ribose + A,G,C,U, single-stranded.
Lipids: glycerol + fatty acids (ester bonds), hydrophobic, 9 kcal/g energy storage.
Enzymes: protein biocatalysts, substrate-specific, optimum ~37°C, reusable, lower activation energy.
Water: ~70–80% of protoplasm, dipolar universal solvent.
summary: Life is composed of organic (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids) and inorganic (water, minerals) components. Carbohydrates (Cn(H2O)n) store and provide energy; amino acids join by peptide bonds to form proteins with four structural levels; lipids (ester-linked, hydrophobic) store energy at 9 kcal/g and build membranes; nucleic acids carry heredity (DNA double helix) and drive protein synthesis (RNA). Enzymes are specific, reusable protein catalysts with optimum temperature and pH. DNA vs RNA differ in sugar (deoxyribose/ribose), bases (thymine/uracil), and strand nature.
